chapter: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
title: Jelly Roll Morton, the Lion's piano night and Joe Jordan
summary: Whaley remembers Jelly Roll outside the Lafayette, piano night at the Famous Door with the Lion and James P. Johnson, Joe Jordan, and the need to read music.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Jelly Roll Morton, I used to meet him in front of the Lafayette Theatre, had his music under his arm, walking up and down, said he was going to make it one day. Jelly Roll Morton.
What kind of dude was he.
Oh, he was a great guy, see, always saying he's going to make it.
He bragged a lot but he proved it, didn't it.
Yeah, he proved it. He could do it.
How about -- didn't you run into the Lion about that time.

Oh, yeah, the Lion, the Lion used to -- they used to have a place on 129th Street and Tremont -- no, and what's that main street in New York. Seventh Avenue, used to call the Famous Door and every Monday night, it was piano night. Duke, Jimmie J.P. Johnson, Dan Carey, Joe Burrow, all them piano players, they'd come down and the Lion, the Lion would have his derby and a cigar and tap you on the shoulder, 'hey, I'll take it.'
Time for you to get up. What year was that.
Duke used to go down there too.
Oh, yeah, Duke was down there. J.P. Johnson, would play a number 32 choruses and not one chorus the same.
They tell me he was really great.
Oh, he was great, and I used to sit back there and listen to all of them. Joe Jordan, did you ever know Joe Jordan.
Yes, didn't he come in from Chicago.
Yeah, he was over in Europe and he made enough money gambling and he came in and built that building in Chicago, named it the Jordan Building. He just died here recently.
Yeah, he was out there -- where did he go, he went out west. Yeah, he went out west somewhere. Out in Seattle, that's where he was, up there in Seattle.

I used to tell the fellows you got to learn to read that music, because Fletcher Henderson had one of the greatest bands and he missed a job because the fellows couldn't read the music. There was only five fellows that could read music, right here in New-York.
